o: The min-product of a subarray is its minimum element times its sum, and we maximize this over all non-empty contiguous subarrays, applying the 10^9 + 7 modulus only at the very end. In [1,2,3,2] the window [2,3,2] has minimum 2 and sum 7, giving 14; in [2,3,3,1,2] the pair [3,3] gives 3 * 6 = 18. Because all values are positive, widening a window while its minimum stays the same only adds mass to the sum — so for every element it suffices to consider the MAXIMAL span in which it remains the minimum. That is exactly the largest-rectangle-in-histogram setup with prefix sums playing the role of widths, solvable with a monotonic stack in linear time; the intuitive O(n^2) running-min double loop is fine as a baseline but strains at n up to 3*10^4.
k: Positive values mean extending a window never hurts while the minimum is unchanged — maximal spans dominate all subarrays.
For each index i, the best window where nums[i] is the minimum runs from the previous strictly smaller element to the next strictly smaller one; a monotonic stack finds these bounds in O(n).
Do arithmetic in 64-bit (sums reach ~3*10^11 and products ~10^18) and apply the modulus only after choosing the maximum.

a.i: Fix each left endpoint and extend the right end, maintaining the running sum and running minimum; every subarray min-product is evaluated this way. Direct and correct, but quadratic.
s: For each left index i, reset total = 0 and mn = infinity.
Grow j from i rightward, adding nums[j] to total and updating mn.
Track mn * total against the best after each extension.
a.t: O(n^2) — each left endpoint extends a running sum and minimum over all right ends; too slow near n = 3*10^4

a.n: Approach 2: Monotonic Stack Over Maximal Spans
a.i: Build prefix sums so any window sum is a subtraction. Sweep indices left to right keeping a stack of positions with increasing values; when the current value drops below the stack top (a sentinel 0 at index n flushes everything), the popped element h is the minimum of the maximal span from just above the next remaining stack entry through i - 1, so evaluate h * (pre[i] - pre[l]) where l is that boundary plus one. Popping on >= lets equal neighbours still hand the full window to the last of them, so the optimum is always evaluated.
s: Compute pre[0..n] with pre[i+1] = pre[i] + nums[i].
Scan i from 0 to n with cur = nums[i], or 0 as sentinel at i = n.
While the stack top value >= cur, pop h; let l be (new top) + 1 or 0 if empty; update best with h * (pre[i] - pre[l]).
a.t: O(n) — every index is pushed once and popped at most once from the monotonic stack
a.sp: O(n) — prefix-sum array and the stack

w: State the maximal-window argument, then implement the single-pass stack version. Pitfalls: forgetting the sentinel flush at index n, popping with > instead of >= so tied minimums never get their full window, doing modular reduction too early (the true maximum must fit in 64 bits before modding), and overflowing 32-bit sums in C++/Java. Follow-ups: report the winning subarray bounds (record boundaries when updating the best), support point updates (segment tree merging minimum and sum), or handle non-positive values, which breaks the extension argument.
